newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Independent tv network finally on air in Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: Independent tv network finally on air in Bosnia.

text.p: Bosnia's much-delayed independent television network hit the airwaves this weekend with amateurish news reporting and a Tina Turner concert, but critics said it had begun too late to influence elections.
The Open Broadcast Network (OBN) -- an internationally funded network which groups five local, non-nationalist tv stations -- aired its maiden three-hour show on Saturday night.

Two of the stations are in the capital Sarajevo and one each in Zenica, Tuzla and east Mostar, all within Moslem-ruled Bosnian federation territory. Regions of Bosnia run by Serb or Croat separatists took no interest in the project.

OBN was conceived by the international community to inject some press freedom into an overwhelmingly state-run media environment in the approach to the September 14 elections mandated by the 1995 Dayton peace treaty.

The office of Carl Bildt, international peace coordinator in Bosnia, committed some $10 million for a network designed to offset nationalist state media that depict political opposition as "enemies of the homeland" to intimidate voters.
Each OBN station uses modernised equipment provided by international donors but there were last-minute shortages of basic items like microphones, underlining the slap-dash inception of the project.

Saturday's opening show seemed amateurish with awe-struck commentary from a young Sarajevo reporter entering Serb territory under apparent international escort, and messily edited camera shots marred by errant microphones.

Most Serbs refused to speak to the woman reporter except for an old farmer in Foca and two teenagers in Visegrad who daringly said it was time for Bosnia's communities to live together in peace again.

In the federation town of Bugojno, run by hardline Moslem nationalists, a man with his face blacked out for anonymity accused the local leadership of ethnic discrimination and a Croat woman said relations with Moslems were dire.

Next came an interview in Sarajevo with visiting emigre Serb businessman Milan Panic, briefly Serbian prime minister in 1992, who said the elections were vital to reunify Bosnia. But Panic would have been a stranger to most viewers.

Broadcasters say the network's signal probably reaches over 50 percent of Bosnia, and more with the help of satellite dishes. But critics said OBN probably hit the airwaves too late to make a democratic impact on the election.

Bildt, the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe -- which is supervising the elections -- and the commander of Bosnia's NATO-led peace force rebuked the Bosnian government last month for impeding efforts to set up OBN.
Diplomats said Moslem authorities had gone out of their way to prevent the OBN going on air with shared programming.

Elvir Svrakic of independent Hayat TV in Sarajevo said the network's hub was temporarily blocked off by state police claiming the building was reserved for a public school, although it never had been.
The government has also failed to act on repeated Bildt requests for an official frequency and broadcast licence, leaving it vulnerable to arbitrary shutdown.
Bosnian officials have denied being opposed to OBN news programmes but said they objected to its plan for extended entertainment programmes with commercials.
Independent observers said the hostility of the Serbs and Croats to the network was a serious setback.
